newsitem.title: USA: Lima drama has eerie parallels with Bogata crisis.
newsitem.headline: Lima drama has eerie parallels with Bogata crisis.

text.p: The hostage drama in Lima brings back memories to former U.S. ambassador Diego Asencio of his own ordeal in the Dominican Embassy residence in Bogota in 1980.
In that episode, he and his fellow hostages negotiated their own release with Colombian M-19 guerrillas and were released after 61 days.
His advice to the hostages in Lima -- keep yourselves mentally and physically active to avoid falling into despair.
To President Alberto Fujimora: "No government with respect for the rule of law can afford to release prisoners on demand to terrorists."

Asencio, in an article he wrote in Sunday's Miami Herald, said he felt a sense of deja vu when he heard that Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas had stormed a glitzy party at the Japanese ambassador's residence and taken a host of dignatories hostage on Tuesday night.

"The assault on an embassy reception, the shoot-out, the demand for the release of political prisoners, the threat to begin killing hostages, the beginning of jockeying among countries as attempts are made to reconcile differing positons on terrorism....

"It brought back fresh memories of gunfire, sprawled bleeding bodies and the shock to one's system as the physiological processes slowed down. Fortunately, the numbness also ensured an almsot surreal lack of fear. It was only when hope returned and one became human again that fear also returned."
He said the Bogota hostages spent long hours talking to the guerrillas, convincing them to shed the "gangster mentality" and to start thinking like politicians.

A deal was worked out in which fair trials under international monitoring would be guaranteed for the political prisoners which M-16 wanted released. The hostages, guerrillas and mediators were flown to Havana in a Cuban plane sent by President Fidel Castro.
"It worked and we see no reason why, in view of the eerie similarities between the two episodes, the same solution would not serve," Asencio said.
The hostages in Lima are suffering from lack of food and water and cramped, insanitary conditions.
In Bogota, Asencio wrote, the Israeli ambassador organised the hostages for housekeeping duties.
"This not only kept their surroundings acceptably clean, but it kept up their morale."
The hostages also reviewed drafts of a deal and discussed them at length with their captives.
"Both during the captivity and the aftermath those persons who kept occupied fared better than those who succumbed to depression and inactivity," he said.
